utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Egbers. Please sit down. Welcome back to the courtroom. Thank you very much that you could make it again. And I should say to the interpreters, welcome to the Tribunal, especially those who are interpreting into Dutch. May I remind you that your affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And if I'm not mistaken, we are still in cross-examination. Good morning, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace in this house. I would like the day to end today just like all days, in accordance with God's will and not as I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome Mr. Egbers, and I hope today we will finish his cross-examination. Mr. Egbers, last time we stopped when you were talking about how you were disarming Muslims when you noticed that they had weapons, and I quoted the statement by Mr. Franken where he said that you could not enter their homes without the agreement of the police. Could you please explain the difference in the statements between you and Mr. Franken, and can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this difference actually was all about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Part of the statement by Major Franken was read by you, in which you said that he had a problem when our troops went after armed Muslims. I said, after that, that in reality, in actual fact, our special forces went after the people who at times fled into houses. I don't see such a big problem between what may happen and what did happen. Have I answered your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, you answered my question. If you can answer this question too: Were you able to enter the homes without the consent of their Muslim owners in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, did not go after armed Muslims, but I know that our special forces did do that and also went into a house. I cannot say whether formally it was done correctly, formally, but that it did happen in the past. These are questions that you should have asked Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, that's correct. I would just like to ask you this: Did you ever see soldiers of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR enter a house, and did they ever bring back to their base a rifle or a weapon that they had seized in the home of a Muslim civilian? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. I only heard that in other units, not my own platoon, that it happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if, before you came to the enclave, you were familiar with the historical events that had happened in the enclave, the ones that preceded the demilitarisation, and what happened in the process of demilitarisation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were trained to think differently and, instead of acting as a soldier, more as a peacekeeper. It was also said to us which conflicts were in course in the Balkans. But what exactly was happening before we came, in relation to demilitarisation, this was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your sincere answer. Can you please tell me if you knew what the provisions were of this demilitarisation agreement that applied to the Srebrenica zone, what it implied, and what were the obligations of UNPROFOR members in terms of that agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, as platoon commander, I was responsible for the platoon of UNPROFOR soldiers. We were manning the Alpha Observation Post. In walking in the area of OP -- there were patrols in the area of OP Alpha. If we were to come across armed Muslims in the enclave, then our order was to seize the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us this: If the Muslims prevented you from doing this, what did you do then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could prevent me from disarming them by running away. What we then did was go after them. But in general, it only happened rarely that in the enclave, we saw Muslims openly carrying weapons. This only happened during the attack on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us why, then, you were not permitted to enter the Bandera Triangle? How were you supposed to implement this demilitarisation if you were denied access? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole question of the Bandera Triangle was, in January 1995, as you know, it was a reaction to the reduction in size of the enclave, which was happening continuously because of the BSA approaching. When our -- when UNPROFOR's reaction, in the eyes of the Muslims, appeared not to be sufficient, they barred us access to the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying that on the basis of information about your activities or on the basis of UNPROFOR information that Serbs were attacking and reducing the size of the enclave in that area where you were patrolling? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the information that UNPROFOR command line, the chain of command, received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you check whether this was true or not? Were the Serbs attacking this part of the Bandera Triangle or were they ever in this Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they were in the Bandera Triangle, but the Serbians were shifting up towards the enclave, which made the life in that part of the enclave more difficult because they could come under direct fire from the Bosnian Serbs. I was a lieutenant, a platoon commander, and I did not have the possibility to see whether the Bosnian Serbs had shifted in the direction of the enclave. I have to base myself on what the battalion leadership told me, what I heard from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This was something that the battalion commander told you, but what I'm asking you is this: Was there any kind of conflict waged between Serbs and Muslims in the Bandera Triangle and on the edges of the triangle up until that point in time when you were no longer permitted to patrol the Bandera area?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- between Muslims inside the enclave and the Bosnian Serbs outside the enclave, between them there was constant conflict in the area of OP Alpha. Nearly daily there was shooting in that area, both from inside the enclave and outside, so by Bosnian Serbs shooting at Muslims and sometimes from inside the enclave back to the Bosnian Serbs. It was a very restless part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us if that was specifically the reasons why the Serbs carried out the operation to separate the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, because the Muslims considered that area safe and used it as a corridor in order to get supplies and weapons into the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enclave of Zepa is in the south of Srebrenica, and the Bandera Triangle is to the west of the enclave. Therefore, if Muslims from Srebrenica were to walk from Srebrenica to Zepa, it would be to the south of the enclave, where UNPROFOR was. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is so, then why would the Serbs fire into the northern part of the enclave, which is called the Bandera Triangle, if the Muslims were arming themselves from the south? Are you able to explain that to the Trial Chamber, or do you have a certain confirmation, or are you only saying this on the basis of your thinking and your own conclusions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 6th of January, 1995, I was in the enclave, and it was always restless in the west part of the enclave. It's not that there was complete peace there. There was shooting, both shooting at UNPROFOR soldiers or above our heads, their heads, our heads. Muslims reacted. This always was a restless part of the enclave, and that was in the west. This is what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell the Chamber, would the Muslims have driven you out of an area in which they were attacking Serbs, so that you wouldn't see that, and is it true that in the beginning -- later, they were driving you to go in front of them to wage battle against the Serbs instead of them? Does this sound logical at all to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little activity was observed in the Bandera Triangle. Of course, we were aware of shooting, and we reported on this. You must certainly have information on this or be able to find it. But what struck us is that OP Alpha, it was always restless around OP Alpha. The Bandera Triangle, which was just to the south of it, was less restless. The second part of your question, you say that the Serbians pushed us ahead of them in order to attack Bosnian Serbians? Could you please explain this more clearly? I can't quite follow the logic here. Are you speaking about July 1995, the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm talking about a certain part of the enclave, and I'm saying that the Muslims were placing you in front of them and making you fight instead of them so that they could protect the enclave. Perhaps you received the wrong interpretation. I'm asking you whether the Muslims were driving you in certain areas in front of them to fight instead of them and were not allowing you access to the Bandera Triangle, where they actually were fighting the Serbs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with the words used, that we were driven ahead by Bosnian Muslims in order to fight against the Serbs. I simply cannot understand what you are trying -- where you are going with this. Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to be more specific. When you said that you went four kilometres ahead of the Muslims and that one of your patrol leaders was captured when he was seeking the Serbs, that you had to go there because the Muslims were telling you to go ahead after you left the check-point, do you recall that part of your statement? Thank you. I don't want to be quoting your statement back to you now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I think it would be helpful for at least the record to reflect whether General Tolimir is talking about the witness's OTP statement or whether he's talking about prior testimony. He refers here to a statement, but I don't know whether he's, in fact, referring to some other statement, whether it's an OTP statement or perhaps a debriefing statement, and I think it would be helpful if whatever the source of this question is is shown to the witness. We've had a number of fairly vague questions, in terms of time-period and location. Colonel Egbers has asked for some more specificity. I think it would be helpful for the record if we just had an idea of really what we're talking about here. And my recollection is, is that the portion -- whatever this is that General Tolimir is quoting from is not being quoted accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, which statement do you mean when you were referring to a statement during your last - stop, please, I'm still talking - when you were saying, "I don't want to be quoting your statement back to you now"? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like the Registry to show P1145, document P1145. That is the statement of this witness, Mr. Egbers, that he gave on the 24th of October, 1995, to representatives of this Tribunal. Can we now look at page 3 of that statement, paragraph 3, lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 of paragraph 3. Thank you. In the Serbian, this is probably one paragraph but last, on the same page in the English version. Thank you. I apologise that I have to go back to refresh the recollection of what was already said and I'm wasting time, but it says here, in the third paragraph, which is also the third paragraph in the English, it says here: "In Srebrenica, I saw many armed Muslims," "many armed Muslims," "many," "I recognised anti-tank weapons, RPG-7, and non-automatic fire-arms as well as the AK-47. Some pointed their weapons at us and, by arm movements, made it clear to us that we should continue in a southerly direction. We drove to another four vehicles which belonged to us and which were under the command of Captain Hageman."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would now like to remind Mr. Thayer and the witness -- or I want to ask them whether you said this in your statement or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that this is clear, I understand what you mean. It is the case that at that market, on that day, many people were present who were in total panic and were doing everything they could to have the white UN vehicles stay at the market. They did, indeed, attempt to keep me there at the market. Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct, I mentioned the market. Thank you. I said "market." I don't know how this was interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand exactly what you mean. I can talk about that situation, should you have any questions about it. Could you perhaps repeat the question so that I know exactly what your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egbers. I don't need you to speak again about the situation that you already spoke about. All I want to do is ask you whether the Muslims forced you towards the south, in the direction of where the Army of Republika Srpska was, or did they tell you to go in the other direction? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing they did at that point in time was, the south of the market, that big square, the only thing they did was keep us there, detain us there. So not leave them, to drive south. No, precisely to stay with them on the market square, and that was at the southern part of the market square.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am forced, then, to read out that whole part of your statement so that you can be reminded. I don't want to be playing here. I quote: "We drove to another four vehicles which belonged to us and which were under the command of Captain Hageman. He told me over the radio that he was under fire by the local Muslim fighters and, therefore, he could not move his vehicles. The Muslim population was panicking. People climbed into my vehicle. I was driving an APC at that moment. I decided to follow on behind the other vehicles so that I could offer some cover if there was an attack. "We stayed there the whole night. The promised air-strike did not take place." And so on, end of quote. Did you stay at the market all night or did you stay at the positions all night? Can you please tell this to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the market of Srebrenica all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you were not looking for the Serbian Army, as you said the last time, and you did not go to this place where a patrol was captured which had been looking for the Serbs on the 9th and the 10th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which patrol you're referring to. What I can tell you is that I drove on to the market, and during the day-time I saw thousands of people there who tried to keep me at the market. I drove to the south of the market. People stayed there during the evening and the night. Some people left. I stayed there the entire night on the square. The next morning, I was ordered to drive to Bravo 1. And behind the market, there were high hills towards the south. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Evidently, I need to remind you of another part of your statement from the time before, and it's quite a challenge to conduct a cross-examination after a break because you don't recall what happened the first time around.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at page 2 in the e-court, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that Colonel Egbers is a grown man and an experienced officer, but I just want to sort of set down a marker from our position, that these kinds of comments are not helpful, and I'd like to see them stop now, suggestions that the witness needs his recollection refreshed after the break when, frankly, there hasn't been any suggestion of that. It's, frankly, the accused's misreading of these statements that's causing this, and I think it should just stay there and we don't need comments about the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, put your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, you said a moment ago that you were not driven toward the south of the area, but, rather, to the south of the market. I'd like to read out for you what you said on page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 from the bottom: "The next day, Sunday, 9 July 1995, two British SASs arrived. They requested a Netherlands forward air control. Sergeant Bosch and his crew drove to the southern part of the enclave to find out where the Bosnian Serbs were." My question is: Were the Serbs in the south, and was that an area indicated to you by the Muslims as one where you should head to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph is about an observation that I had when I was at Blocking Position 1. Blocking Position 1, as I told you last time, a group which was led by Sergeant Bosch was instructed to go to the Swedish shelter project, which is also in the south of the enclave, and this is quite different from what happened on the market square. Of course, they're both in the south. But this sergeant, with his soldiers, went to the Swedish shelter project, which is much towards the south-west of the enclave. And your question was -- let me see. Let me read it out, whether Muslims had told us whether there were Serbs. Well, from Blocking Position 1, I had an excellent view of what was going on in the south. And I told you earlier on about setting fire to houses and searching houses in Pusmulici, and I saw tanks driving into the enclave and also driving out of the enclave. But the view of what was going on in the Swedish shelter, we did not have a view of what was going on in the Swedish shelter, which is why Captain Groen sent the people to Sergeant Bosch to go to the Swedish shelter, which is another situation than the situation you just described. Did I answer your question correctly or sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egbers. I don't want to dwell on the issue anymore. Let the Trial Chamber assess this point. Let's move on. We lost some time there. Did you know that there were no Serbs at all around the enclave shortly before the attack on the enclave, and that they did not pose a threat to the enclave at all, since they did not build up their forces there, until, that is, the Muslims started attacking Serb-controlled territory out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You raised a number of questions in one go. The first part of your question concerns the presence of Serbian troops around the enclave. I can tell you that they were always there for as long as I was there. The second part of your question, you say that they didn't pose a threat to the enclave and that there was no build-up of troops. Well, indeed, I had no information on the build-up of Bosnian Serb troops in the south of the enclave. It was only afterwards, after the fall of the enclave, that I talked to Major Zoran about this, and he told me that with -- he had left Srebrenica with people from Sarajevo. About the attack by Muslims on Serbian-controlled area outside the enclave, the last part of your question, you will have to be a bit more specific, because what do you mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egbers. It is not my intention to go into the territory that we've already covered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 1D323 in e-court. Thank you. Can we call up 1D323. The document does not have an English translation, so I'll read it out for you. It's a document which, as you can see in the heading, it was drafted on the 28th of June by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was sent to the 2nd Corps Command. We will see that it was signed by the chief of the staff, Brigadier-General Enver, who reported on the information gathered by scouts around Srebrenica. The title is "Intelligence." It says: "Several members of the BH Army who had crossed over from the Srebrenica territory moved along the Srebrenica-Zepa-Radava-Veliki Zep- Mekote-Donja Medja-Visocnik-Pjenovac-Nevacka-Rjecice-Donja Brdo-Sokoline route and across the Jezernica River to the tunnel in Kladanj. On their way, they did not spot any Chetnik formations or fire positions. According to their information, there are no elite units or large military formations around Srebrenica. More than 50 per cent of trenches stand empty and the lines are manned mostly by elderly men. On the Han Pijesak-Sarajevo road, on the 21st and 22nd June 1995, they observed very intensive -- or busy traffic in both ways. "In the night between the 21st and the 22nd of June, 1995, they spotted a column of 12 trailer trucks covered in tarpaulin who -- which was escorted by the military and civilian police details, apparently carrying a large cargo in the direction of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was sent for the information to the 28th Division. Since we can see, based on this document, that there were no forces around Srebrenica and that apparently the Serbs at the time were shipping their forces towards Sarajevo, did UNPROFOR have information at the time about the build-up of forces around Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, I think after the word -- no need for correction. Thank you very much. It was already corrected. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just relying on the LiveNote translation, because we don't have an English translation of the document, but I would ask that that question be corrected, because there is, from the question -- or from the reading of the document, there is no suggestion that there were no troops around the Srebrenica enclave, as General Tolimir is trying to imply. If we look at the route that's described here, and I don't think there's going to be any dispute about this, we're talking about one direction of travel by this group of scouts from the western part of the enclave to the area of Zepa, and that is what this document is reporting. Again, I don't have an English translation, but simply based on the reading of the document, that would seem to be what it indicates, that a group of scouts moved west along this route from Srebrenica to Zepa, not all the way around the enclave, and this document should, therefore, be quoted correctly and not in a misleading manner to suggest what General Tolimir tried to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, this is your position, but the question is quite simple. The question was: "Did UNPROFOR have information at the time about the build-up of forces around Srebrenica?" And I would like to ask the witness to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, as lieutenant and platoon command, I didn't have any information whatsoever regarding the build-up of troops around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Egbers. Can we now show document D53 in e-court. And can the earlier document be admitted into evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D132, Your Honours, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now show Exhibit D53. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to appear: It's a document which was sent to the 28th Division in Srebrenica by the chief of the staff of the 2nd Corps, Dudakovic, Sulejman, on the 17th of June, 1995. It is titled "Preparations for Offensive Combat Activities: Order." And I quote: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, Army General Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the Command of the Protection Regiment in Han Pijesak is holding parts of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa, I hereby issue the following order: "1. Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of BH --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have to slow down. It is impossible for the all interpreters to translate into different languages if you read at this speed. Please slow down, and carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So I'll re-read item 1 for the sake of the interpreters: "1. Execute all preparations within the Command of the 28th Division of the ground forces to engage in offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a view to over-extending the aggressor forces and inflicting losses on them, engage in co-ordinated action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the general Sarajevo area. "2. Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success, on the basis of an accurate assessment and the potential of our forces in Srebrenica and Zepa. "3. The General Staff or the Main Staff of the BH Army will regulate, by an order, the commencement of offensive combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the 28th Army Division."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Does it follow from this document that the army general, Rasim Delic, both verbally and in writing through his subordinates, announced the commencement of offensive combat operations from Srebrenica and Zepa; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I've seen this, and just like anyone else here in the courtroom, the answer that I could give to -- yeah, as you've read it, the only answer possible would be, yes, I've never seen this before. I understand that you want to bring this in and want to involve me in this, but I can have nothing more to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do forces engage in the defence effort or carry out offensive combat activities, or is it done by those that have free forces at their disposal to engage in attacks? I'm asking you from the military point of view, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's possible to perform offensive activities within a defensive activity or task in order to bind the troops, but this is a remark purely as a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document we've just read out, does Rasim Delic refer to the activities taking place in Sarajevo and the assistance that ought to be provided to the forces in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're presenting a document to me that I've never seen before, never studied, and you're asking me substantive questions about this document. Am I the right person to be answering such questions or should you speak to the person who wrote this document, this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Whenever you're unable to answer, just say so. I'm not able to answer this because I didn't author the document, and I won't mind. Do you know that the Muslims around Sarajevo, at the time this document was written, engaged in offensive combat activities; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing I can say about this, because after 15 years, it's not completely clear to me. I don't know. I would have to look it up. I can imagine that it's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. No, there's no need for you to answer that if you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D52 shown up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have D52 on our screens yet. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a memo from the BH Army, its 2nd Corps Command, dated the 8th of July, 1995. In other words, it was written after the order for offensive combat activities. This document was signed by Commander Sead Delic from Tuzla. He says: "Information or report on combat results of the units and commands of the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army." He goes on to say, and I'm quoting: "The soldiers of the 28th Division of the army, stationed in Srebrenica and Zepa, although completely encircled and confronting huge problems relating to survival and the obligation to protect the free territory, committed to contributing, as far as possible, to the struggle against the aggressor, stepped up their activities in the depth of the temporarily occupied territory. An additional motivation for the activities of the members of the 28th Division was the need to prevent the enemy forces from sending in reinforcements from the area around Srebrenica and Zepa to the Sarajevo battle-field by causing losses, primarily those of troops, which will force the aggressor to tie up their troops in the general area of Srebrenica and Zepa. "With this aim, a series of successful sabotage actions were carried out deep in the temporarily occupied territory, where the following results were achieved:" Now I'll just read the first bullet point: "Sixty Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." The text goes on to talk about the items captured and so on. Then the next paragraph says: "In the village of Visnjica, large quantities of ammunition were seized, but the soldiers were exhausted and could not pull those out, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor might use for military purposes." This is my question: Does the 2nd Corps commander, Sead Delic, speak in this report of the successful actions conducted by the defence forces of Srebrenica and Zepa in destroying the surrounding villages and causing civilian losses, with a view to making sure that the troops deployed in that area would not be redeployed to the Sarajevo front-line? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is talking about Chetniks, uses the term. Bosnian Serbs are meant by this, clearly. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter could not hear what was just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, a part of your answer was not interpreted into English. Could you perhaps repeat it? We've only received a translation of: "Yes, he is talking about Chetniks, he uses the term. Bosnian Serbs are meant by this, clearly. And ..." The rest was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that the -- my answer to the rest of the question is, Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the 2nd Corps commander of the BH Army speak of the offensive carried out of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These losses that were inflicted, were they huge? There are other documents where they speak of the losses inflicted, in terms of 15, 20. Here, they refer to the number 60, and it's a document dated the 8th of July. And I chose this document deliberately because it originates from the period when the relevant events in Srebrenica and Zepa transpired, ones that you participated in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking whether the results were enormous. Sixty people -- liquidating sixty people is an enormous result, if that is what you're asking, so the answer can only be, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it not transpire, from the documents written by the Muslims, that these were mostly civilians from the surrounding villages and that one of these villages was burned to the ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to interpret that. What I see is that -- what is written there is that there was ammunition destroyed, that 60 Chetniks -- I assume that these are Bosnian Serbs, that they are what is meant. And whether they are military people or civilians, I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I read in paragraph 3 that the document said that all the facilities that the aggressor might use for military purposes were destroyed in the village of Visnjica, but that doesn't matter. We're not here to justify the actions by either the Muslims or Serbs. Did UNPROFOR at the time, in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, have information about the combat activities taking place around Sarajevo and from demilitarised zones?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR had the information, and it was shared with the UNPROFOR units in Srebrenica. We received an update about the situation in the entire area around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Had the zone been demilitarised pursuant to the agreement, could the Muslims have been attacking from within that zone which was demilitarised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Formally, all weapons had been handed over. But as I said to you, at the end of the enclave, many Muslim fighters were seen by me with weapons, so the zone was not totally demilitarised. There were weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that all the weapons had been handed in. That's why I'm forced to quote to you again what the commander of those forces said, the forces that had handed over their weapons. Mr. Naser Oric -- this is document D126.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see this in e-court. It says: "It was important to us --" I quote. Thank you. I apologise, and now we see it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is asked to repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you please repeat the reference, because that was not translated and your microphone was off at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is document -- well, this is a tell-all, an interview by Naser Oric after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, where he's talking, in the last two paragraphs, about how he handed over the weapons to UNPROFOR. And the witness now just said that all the weapons had been handed over to UNPROFOR. Can we look at page 3 in the English, please, and can we show the last two paragraphs. And now we see this third page in the English as well, where it says: "'We did not want the Chetniks to see the weapons that we had not handed over. That would be an argument for them to refuse to sign the agreement or to do who knows what. We had some 2.000 barrels. I knew that for sure. And I did not know everything. Weapons were being hidden. We kept some 20 cannons, 20/1, with four barrels, which we turned into single-barrel cannon, so in the end they were used as a kind of anti-aircraft guns. Let me explain, actually. Each single barrel that we managed to capture from the Chetniks, we would hide. And when we would be going out for an action, we would take them out. Everybody hid weapons from everyone else. Only the bold ones reported them, the real soldiers. The others would hide them until they were needed. All of this is understandable. We probably had some 4.000 barrels, thus, which became evident during the breakthrough towards Tuzla. This is without counting the brigade in Zepa .'"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the basis of this text, my question to you is: Can it be seen that all of the weapons were handed over to you or whether the Muslims hid some of the weapons after the demilitarisation of the zone, according to we have seen that Naser Oric has said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to go back to what you have repeated twice, two minutes past 10.00, line 12, as if I was saying that all weapons had been handed over. I only said that there was a weapon collection point where weapons were lying and that this -- apart from that, Bosnian Muslims had weapons available. If we saw them, we tried to confiscate them. And at the end of the enclave, I saw many Muslims walking with weapons. I already stated this. I did not say that all weapons had been handed in, and this is clear. This is a remark I want to make. You were speaking as if I assume that all weapons had been handed in, and we can see clearly together that this is not the case. On the basis of the text, you are asking whether weapons could have been hidden. I think that was the case. Am I answering your question sufficiently with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's sufficient if you were to tell me whether UNPROFOR, the Dutch Battalion, while it was in Srebrenica, knew that there were some hidden weapons that Naser Oric mentioned in the text we have just read. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew and saw it only at the point in time in which the enclave was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this is so, we're now going to read the last paragraph of this statement that we see here both in English and the Serbian: "As soon as the UNPROFOR set up their check-points, we realised immediately that we could not rely on them. So one whole team of my men, they were not men with military training, but they were reliable and they were part of the reserve units, decided that we would establish our own lines and that we would organise our own observers. The system functioned in the following way: When an UNPROFOR patrol would approach, our guys on the lines would inform us so we could conceal the weapons. If the UNPROFOR soldiers asked us how come these boys were there on those lines, we would answer them that we did not trust them and that we were afraid of Chetniks, and that we wanted to have our own guards. They showed some understanding for that, which was not the case when we dug trenches and fortifications." My question, on the basis of this, is: While you were patrolling in Srebrenica, you members of the DutchBat, did you ascertain that Muslims were staying at positions without weapons when you came along? This both applies to lines and trenches. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At unpredictable times, we came along and we, of course, saw Bosnian Muslims in the area of the boundary of the enclave. I know that a half a year before we came, DutchBat 2, our soldiers, also at that time went into trenches and these spaces there, and that one of our colleagues crawled onto a mine there. So it did take place. If we found weapons, we confiscated them. And as you just read out, those weapons were hidden whenever we came. Have I answered your question sufficiently, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that why you said -- during the examination-in-chief by Mr. Thayer on the topic of these targets, you said people wearing civilian clothing and armed with rifles belonged to groups of Muslims within the enclave. You asked -- actually, you answered this in response to a question by Judge Mindua, when you said that these people in civilian clothing and carrying weapons were from within the enclave. Is that who you meant, that they were from within the Srebrenica enclave, soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at the end of the enclave did I see soldiers walking in uniform. Before that, I saw the Bosnian Muslims, the men, only in civilian clothes, and the weapons I saw only at the end of the enclave, when the enclave was attacked. This is what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall, on page 7152, lines 5 to 9, in response to a question by Judge Mindua, you answered -- when he asked you whether these were Bosnian recruits, you answered that these were people wearing civilian clothing and armed with rifles. On the basis of that, are you able to tell us, if you remember, whether the Muslims only showed the weapons at the end of the conflict which they had been concealing up 'til then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the conflict, as you call it, we saw Muslims wearing or carrying their weapons openly. From January to June, there were no weapons carried openly in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Had the zone been demilitarised pursuant to the agreement, would the Muslims have been able to carry their weapons around or would they have had to conceal them? Can you please answer that question? And in the meantime, can we look at D21 in e-court so that we can see the provision of that particular agreement.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, you want me to choose between carrying openly and hiding, and I am choosing for a third option, and that is handing weapons over to a weapon collection point. And that is what they should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this agreement now, which is on the screen in front of you. You can see that this agreement on the cease-fire in the territory was signed between General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993, in the presence of General Philippe Morillon. Are you aware that at the time, Muslims were overtly attacking from within the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, the territory that was surrounded by Republika Srpska, they did not want to recognise the authorities of Republika Srpska, that they were attacking the villages around the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, they had burned and attacked a number of villages? And a number of documents were shown before the Trial Chamber on these incidents. Are you aware or do you have any knowledge about the attacks that are being referred to here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks of 1993, I do not know. I know they took place, but I can't say which parties -- which party attacked the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Are you aware -- did you ever hear from Nikolic or Vukotic, since you mentioned that they were liaison officers, officers for contact with the UNPROFOR, that 2.800 to 3.200 civilians and soldiers were killed around Srebrenica from the Muslim enclave of Srebrenica, attacks from there, and this was before 19 -- before the signing of this agreement in 1993, so in the course of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in that time, 1992-1993, there was a bloody conflict. The two people that you refer to said nothing to me. I know this from the general open sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were aware of this from open sources, are you aware that this conflict between Serbs and Muslims was halted with the demilitarisation of that area on the 8th of May, 1993? Thank you. Thank you. I correct myself: that the conflict was halted by concluding the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that was the case for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please look at Article 1. That speaks about the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica and Zepa area, and I am quoting: "The demilitarised areas will include the area within the current zones of conflict, lines of conflict. The precise boundaries will be marked by the UNPROFOR commander on the ground after consultations." Thank you. My question from this is this: Was the demilitarisation supposed to occur in the areas that were under the control of UNPROFOR, as is stated in the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please look at Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page of the agreement in the English, please. This is the provision on the demilitarisation. We can see Article 3. It's shown here. It states -- the first sentence states: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is: Had everything been implemented according to this agreement, and had the Muslims handed over their weapons, would then there have been a war waged from within the demilitarised zone with the Serbian Army and population outside of those zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether these articles were respected. The only thing I can say is that I know that the Muslims, in the evenings or nights, did leave the enclave. One Muslim fighter I spoke with showed me proudly a weapon which he had taken from the Bosnian Serbs. This is what I can say about this. In 1993, I was not in the enclave. No Dutch unit was. Weapons were handed in, and it turned out that these were not all the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this was not the first time that the witness provided you with an answer about the demilitarisation and the weapons not being handed over to the UNPROFOR. Do you think it is necessary to dwell on this again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wasn't asking that. I was asking the witness whether the UNPROFOR could have been able to carry out any activities, combat activities, from within the enclave had they handed over all of their weapons. So they can answer with a yes or a no. Thank you. I'm sorry, I misspoke. I said "UNPROFOR," but my question was: Had the Muslims handed over all of their weapons from Srebrenica, would they have been able to carry out any kind of combat actions from within Srebrenica and outside of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you received your answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since they didn't hand everything over, as we heard, are you familiar with Article 60, about demilitarised zones, from the Geneva Conventions, Protocol 1? If you are not -- well, you said you knew the Geneva Conventions. But if not, I'm going to read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was if you are familiar with Article 60 of the Geneva Convention Protocol 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 60. Well, I wouldn't be able to recite it, so I assume that General Tolimir will be reading it out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to be reading Article 60. Article 1 of Article 60 of the demilitarised zone says, I quote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters refer the listeners to the original English of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't have it on the screen. You didn't give a reference with the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is the Geneva Conventions. And we did not provide a translation because there is a text that is present in the courtroom, and the witness said last time that he knew the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. We are going to provide a print-out of that particular article to the witness, to the Prosecution, and also to the Trial Chamber. In Article 2 it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was not the question. We are not asking for a print-out. Can you tell us the number of the document in e-court so that it could be called up. And then you may put your questions. It is much easier if the witness can look at it. What is the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but we did not put the Geneva Conventions in the e-court because these are laws, if I may put it that way, which can be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a complicated course of action. I would suggest to have the first break three minutes earlier, and you should contact your legal assistant to discuss how to proceed if you want to put a question to -- a text to the witness. We'll adjourn and resume at five minutes before 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So let's continue. I see we have a print-out on our desks, but we don't have it on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told this is now seen also on the ELMO, so that everybody can look at it on the screen and on the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will not be reading out the entire Article 60, only item 7, which reads, and I quote: "If one of the parties to the conflict commits a material breach of the provisions of paragraphs 3 or 6, the other party shall be released from its obligations under the agreement, conferring upon the zone the status of demilitarised zone. In such an eventuality, the zone loses its status, but shall continue to enjoy the protection provided by the other provisions of this protocol and the other rules of international law applicable in armed conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: If the Muslim side breached the provisions of the demilitarised agreement, thus committing a material breach of the agreement, the Serbian side, was it duty-bound to honour the status of demilitarised zone, since offensive activities were taking part within it, as we were able to see the surrounding Serb villages were the subject of attacks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I understand that you are asking me whether an attack on the enclave by the Bosnian Serbs was justified?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is my question, in view of the fact that the demilitarisation agreement was breached, through the very fact that attacks were launched on civilians and the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to discuss every article and stipulation leading to a demilitarised zone being there. You are saying that activities were taking place in the enclave towards the outside, but an attack on the enclave could not be justified by that. You are really going to have to speak to legal experts if you wish to know more about this. I can say to you what I experienced, myself, on the ground during the attack on the enclave. I was shot at. If you want to talk about that, then I can answer your questions. If, on the basis of -- if you were justified to do that, on the basis of articles, is a question to be put to legal experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a representative of UNPROFOR, were you aware of the fact that the enclave would be attacked, if attacks are launched from it, if a demilitarised zone is no longer in existence?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that at a higher strategic level you discuss then about the new situation and you discuss with the representatives of the United Nations. I realised that in the enclave, we were not in a position to stop an attack on the enclave. We did not have the weapons, we did not have the personnel. The only thing that we could do was to report the exchange of fire in the area of the enclave so that at another level, decisions could be taken which could lead to a re-establishment of a quiet in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Muslims knew, because they were told by UNPROFOR, that if they continue mounting attacks from the demilitarised zone, this status of the zone would be lifted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up D16 in e-court, and then we will be able to see that even the Muslims, themselves, were fully aware of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to another document, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, Mr. Egbers. Before the Defence counsel moves to another question, or the accused Tolimir, I would like to get back to the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave. I will, of course, not look into the legal qualifications of the terms of the agreement relating to Srebrenica. This is something which the Trial Chamber will do. Nonetheless, I can put questions to you on your actions and your mandate, the one you had been given when you were operating there. So this is my question: Since you were part of UNPROFOR, what did you rely on as regards this demilitarisation? Did you rely on the agreement between the warring parties, which we addressed earlier today? Did you rely on this agreement between the warring parties or did you rely on a decision taken by the Security Council? Who asked you to demilitarise the enclave? This, in essence, is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the enclave, we acted according to the current rules of engagement. The rules of engagement were based on the Security Council, on their resolutions. In the rules of engagement, it was set out when we could act, and what was important there, and I remember this clearly, is the order to only use weapons if UNPROFOR troops were being shot at, themselves. We had no order to defend the enclave. We didn't have the personnel nor the means for this. And in my view, we had a warning function, so that others could support us from the air. And we based ourselves, in the final instance, on the resolution of the Security Council. This agreement, which was come to in 1993, I have never seen it as literally before, but the consequences for the actions of my platoon on the ground is what I saw. Have I answered your question sufficiently, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have fully answered my question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In view of the question put by His Honour Mr. Mindua, can we recall D21 in order for you to see that the agreement does not rule out the relevant Security Council resolution. Quite the contrary, it is quoted in the provisions of the agreement. Thank you. Can we have D21 again, page 2. Thank you. This is the preamble to the agreement. Can we keep the English and call up the Serbian version. Thank you, though we need the page before in both English and Serbian. I will read out what the agreement says, and now we have the right page in English. Paragraph 2 reads: "Reconfirming their will to establish peace within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as stated in the agreement between contracting parties concluded on 8 May 1993. "Reconfirming Resolution 824 of the Security Council, in which is declared that the towns of Zepa and Srebrenica and their surroundings should be treated as safe areas by all the parties concerned and should be free from armed attacks and from any other hostile act."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Does it clearly follow from this that Resolution 824 of the Security Council is incorporated in the agreement, or is it left out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Included in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the next passage, it refers to the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and Protocol 1. They, too, are included in the agreement; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at a document of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina sent to the 2nd Corps Command, the Operational Group Srebrenica Command. This is D16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call it up in e-court, please. Thank you. We have it in the Serbian language. I will be reading from the second paragraph. Now we have it in English as well. I'm reading from paragraph 2, and I quote -- this is a 17 February 1995 document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were quite clear on the fact that they could lose the status of demilitarised zone. So paragraph 2 reads: "We estimate that the aggressor," that's to say, forces of Republika Srpska, "will start offensive combat operations with the aim of completely overpowering the Milici-Podravanje Road, and then attempt to seize the territory of the demilitarised zones. "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor filed a request with UNPROFOR to declare Zepa a non-demilitarised zone, with the following rationale:" Under bullet 1: "Helicopter flights were registered whereby the BH Army was supplying weapons and ammunition." Bullet point 2: "Movements of the BH Army have been registered in the Zepa sector." Bullet point 3: "Accusing members of UNPROFOR for covering up the activities and intentions of the BH Army, which is why they no longer guarantee safety. "On the night between 15 and 16 February, our helicopters were seen flying over and infantry fire was opened on them." Now let's skip the next paragraph and read the first bullet point of the paragraph further down: "A helicopter reconnaissance operation of the protected Zepa zone was scheduled for 17 February 1995, but the aggressor side refused to allow it. "A visit by the Ukrainian Colonel," et cetera, "deputy commander of the UNPROFOR Sarajevo sector, was announced for 18 February 1995 ..." Et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it not follow from this document that the Command of the BH Army was quite clear on the fact that the Serbs were asking for the zone to be proclaimed a non-demilitarised zone because of the activities taking place therein? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that you are showing me shows, indeed, that the enclave of Zepa was discussed. The sentence you read out, you are now asking me a question on that, and my answer is, Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at D67, and you will see that it confirms the veracity of the information concerning helicopter flights. I am not interested in anything else. Thank you. D67. In e-court, you have it before you on the screen. This is a document sent on the 13th of July, 1995, to President Alija Izetbegovic by the General Staff of the BH Army, and was sent through the Intelligence Administration in Sarajevo. All of that you can read in the heading. I will be reading out the fourth bullet point only, which is on the next page in English. Can we have the next page in English shown. Bullet point 4 reads: "In preparations for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff, and the 26th Division Chief of Staff," Naser Oric. It doesn't say that; I added it, "The division commander, who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight, did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained behind." There is mention of 17 helicopter flights through which the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa got weapons supplies. Can we go back to page 1 in both versions in order to look at the second bullet point. It reads: "Seventeen helicopter flights were carried out, in each of which a helicopter was hit."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what I've just read, was any of this known to you, to UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, that the Muslims were getting weapons through Zepa and through the air from Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that from Srebrenica, people were walking on foot to Zepa. I, myself, did not see any helicopter flights, because this, I think, is only about the Zepa enclave. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the commander of the BH Army writing this, who reports to his president that 17 helicopter flights were conducted and that Zepa and Srebrenica were given supplies by helicopter. He also reports on the attempts to bring commanders into Tuzla -- into Srebrenica, that is, by helicopter in order to engage in an operation to link up Zepa and Srebrenica. Can you tell me: If this something you had not seen, does it necessarily mean that it did not happen?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that it did not take place. What I see is that this text is dated the 13th of July, 1993 [as interpreted], a few days after the enclave fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake with the date. It shows clearly that it is 13th of July, 1995, and not 1993, as the answer was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So two days after the enclave was run over. You're saying that helicopter flights took place. I didn't see them. Maybe they went to Zepa. Perhaps you were there at that time. Maybe you can say something about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have no right to testify, but I've shown you a document where the chief of the BH Army, two days after the fall of Srebrenica, reports to his president on the extent of activities taken up in order to reinforce the combat levels in Srebrenica. My question was: Did you, in UNPROFOR, know of any of these activities taking part in the BH Army that were referred to by Rasim Delic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this. I don't know if UNPROFOR knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were not aware of this, can you answer the following question: If the Serbs grant Srebrenica the status of a demilitarised zone, a Srebrenica which was about to fall on 8 May 1993, was it justified for UNPROFOR to tolerate the presence of weapons, not to divulge this, not to prevent this, and thus allowing Muslim-Serb conflicts to take place within the territory of the enclave because there were weapons there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1995, I was in the enclave. I can only answer this question from myself, what I experienced, what I saw. I can't speculate about 1993 to 1995. I don't think UNPROFOR contributed to the development of the conflict between Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry for the intervention, but while we have it up on the LiveNote, at page 40, line 19, I think it's worth putting on the record the following: General Tolimir said: "I have no right to testify." He's made similar statements during the course of the proceedings on other occasions. I just want to make it clear, from the Prosecution's position, that we understand that he has an absolute right to testify as a witness in his own defence, pursuant to Rule 85(C), if he so chooses, and the Prosecution will not do anything to impair that right that he holds as a fundamental right, to testify as a witness in his own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that everybody is aware of this Rule. I was concerned about your formulation as well, because you have the right to testify, but you are not allowed to give evidence while putting questions to a witness. I'm quite sure that I understood your remark in that way, that you are not allowed to give evidence by putting questions. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought that the Prosecutor took it that way as well. But if not, I just want to explain that during questioning, I cannot testify, and the witness knows that as well, since he asked if he may say something. But, in any case, thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, please, during the cross-examination you said, repeatedly, that there were armed civilians who had opposed the organised armed force of the Army of Republika Srpska, and questions were put to you also by Mr. Mindua. My question is: Do you remember that? Do you remember that part of the examination, and do you remember the questions that Judge Mindua put to you on that topic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Should it have been allowed, in the demilitarised zone, for the number of civilians to rise so much, civilians that could have taken part in the armed resistance towards the Army of Republika Srpska? Is that something that should have been allowed to happen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was before my time. I do know that when we came to the enclave, people who were in the enclave were not free to go to Central Bosnia, their own Muslim area. Those who were there had to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether the UNPROFOR should have prevented any kind of armed attacks from within the demilitarised zone, at the areas surrounding the zone, from an area that it had granted the status of a demilitarised zone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units which were there, the UNPROFOR units, could only man observation posts. In my part of the enclave, 50 kilometres perimeter had one observation post from which, together with 12 soldiers, I had to keep an eye on the whole thing. We had no view of what was happening at night or in the evening outside the enclave or within the enclave. We didn't have the personnel. Have I answered your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell me whether the members of UNPROFOR, or its command, or you officers, expected that the Muslims would defend the enclave with arms in the event of an attack? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was this expectation based on; based on the knowledge that they had sufficient weapons or based on something else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I based the expectation on the weapons present at the weapon collection point, and these were maintained faithfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this your personal opinion or is that the opinion of UNPROFOR? I asked whether the UNPROFOR expected the Muslims to defend the enclave with weapons, so I asked whether that was your personal opinion on whether it was the UNPROFOR units that expected that the Muslims would defend themselves with arms in the event the enclave was attacked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at P1148 now, please, page 10 of P1148. Page 10. And then when we see that -- on the basis of that -- P1148, this is an exhibit. Page 10 of that exhibit. This is your interview. We can see page 10 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say: "In the month of May --" This is the text immediately below the first redacted part -- no, actually, after the second redacted part in the English. This is what you say: "An incident occurred in May. The general perception was that the Muslims would defend the enclave themselves and that the UN forces, in that case, could withdraw to blocking positions, but the Muslim defence never came. It was on the basis of this perception that the plan to withdraw was based." My question: In view of the fact that you're talking about the general perception that the Muslims would defend the enclave themselves, was that the general perception prevalent among the DutchBat, as a whole, or was that just your general perception? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I said. It was my perception, because there still were weapons at the weapon collection point. I believe, also, that the battalion commander, Karremans or Franken, opened the weapons collection points for the Muslims when the enclave was attacked, and no weapons were picked up. So these weapons, which had been confiscated and maintained, could have been used in defence. There was no organised defence of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Commander Karremans and Franken, did they open a check-point in May, like you say, or was this in July, and was it the general perception -- that was the general perception of one man or the general perception of all the people who were staying in that area, meaning UNPROFOR representatives? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapon collection point was opened in July for the first, but earlier statements have been made about this. My perception was that the Muslims would defend the enclave. I can't speak for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: And is this why the UNPROFOR took up blocking positions, in order to enable the Muslims to carry out their defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the reason why blocking positions were taken. As a military person, if an attack were to be -- had to be held back, an attack at this scale, I would need anti-tank weapons with a long range, tanks, and air support, artillery, mortars. This would have been a large-scale military operation. This is not something that you can do with just a rifle. We were there in the blocking positions to show that there was a new line had been drawn and that everything to the south of that blocking position was in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Last time, I read to you what Major Franken, as deputy commander, said about the green order. Can you please tell me, the open conflict between UNPROFOR and the Army of Republika Srpska, was that precisely there in order to enable the Muslims to defend the enclave or was this something that happened for a different reason? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting of -- at UNPROFOR soldiers by the Republika Srpska, the BSA, cannot be seen apart from an attack on the total enclave. Only once our soldiers were shot at by the Bosnian Serbians did they become a party to the conflict. I cannot speak about any other defence of Bosnian Muslims, apart from one thing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which only ever shot that one time, artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You now use the term "conflict between the Serbs and UNPROFOR." Please, is an air-strike and three-day green order, was that -- that occurred because you were attacked once by a single tank shell or were you attacked every day? And in your testimony, you showed only such one attack in which you guided an air-strike at a Serbian air tank -- at a Serbian tank --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of what Mr. Tolimir said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreter didn't catch the last part of your question. You're only recorded having said: "In your testimony, you showed only such one attack in which you guided an air-strike at a Serbian tank ..." And then the rest was not heard. Perhaps you can complete your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the question, I further explained that an APC or a tank crew guided an aeroplane to strike at tanks of the Serbian Army that were at a distance of up to two kilometres, and I asked the witness whether it was just that incident that was the basis for a three-day conflict between the Army of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are describing is close air support on the 11th of June, the date on which the enclave fell. We -- two F-16s assisted us there. I then went to Potocari with all the refugees, and there I heard that the threats by the Bosnian Serbian Army was such that we had to stop our military activity immediately. I'm talking about one day in which there was close air support. And I was shot at by a tank more than -- several times. I've given a statement about this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you talked about this earlier, we will leave it up to the Trial Chamber to judge. Anyway, can you please tell us here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
